newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arabs and Jews gloomily await summit end.
newsitem.headline: Arabs and Jews gloomily await summit end.

text.p: Palestinians stood in silent protest and Israelis marched through Jerusalem on Wednesday, wondering whether their leaders could agree to salvage Middle East peace at an emergency White House summit.
Arab expectations that President Bill Clinton could reconcile Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israel's new conservative prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu were low.
Israeli media talked of a crisis in the Washington talks.
Israeli Army radio reported that Palestinians had insisted Israeli withdraw its troops from most of Hebron while rejecting Israeli demands for new security arrangements in the West Bank city.
Ahmed Tibi, an adviser to Arafat, accused Netanyahu of trying to rewrite the 1993 Oslo accords on Palestinian self-rule signed by the previous centre-left Labour government.

"There is an impression that the Israeli delegation and Mr Netanyahu are trying to reformulate the Olso Accords. Almost all of the Palestinian demands, if not all, have been rejected. And I hope, I hope that this picture will change despite the signs are not looking good," Tibi said.

Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said in remarks broadcast on Israeli radio and television: "I hope in Washington they'll find a formulation that will enable a return to the talks table to find solutions to the complicated situation that has been created here. I think it is possible to find formulas."
Palestinian youths threw stones at Israeli soldiers in occupied Hebron when a curfew was briefly lifted but protests in the Israeli-blockaded West Bank and Gaza Strip were generally peaceful.

Traffic came to a halt for five minutes at noon in a strike against Israel's closure of Palestinian-ruled areas since last week's gunbattles and clashes in which 57 Arabs and 15 Israeli soldiers died.
Pedestrians also stopped in a moment of silence. The standstill was reminiscent of the shutdown Israel observes for victims of its wars and the Nazi Holocaust.

Thousands of Israelis and foreign Jews marched to the Wailing Wall for the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles, an annual religious pilgrimage which this year took on political overtones because of the unprecedented fighting.

A steady stream went through the narrow entrance to a controversial archaeological tunnel beside the wall. Netanyahu's decision to open another entrance to the tunnel from Arab Jerusalem's Moslem Quarter ignited already smouldering Arab anger into stone-throwing and then gunbattles.
At a rally some Israelis held banners reading: "Hebron is ours forever".

Hebron, a city holy to Moslems and Jews, is one of the hottest issues on the table at the summit. Arafat insists Netanyahu honour his predecessor's pledge to redeploy troops in the city, home to 100,000 Arabs and fewer than 400 militant Jewish settlers and students.
Soldiers briefly lifted a curfew in Hebron for Arabs to buy supplies on Wednesday.

"The situation in Hebron is tragic. The city has been under curfew for the past seven days which has paralysed life and turned it into a ghost town. The only ones moving in Hebron are the settlers. Any Palestinian who moves out gets detained and is beaten by soldiers," mayor Mustafa Natsheh told Reuters.
Hebron settler leader Noam Arnon said he expected Netanyahu to keep an election pledge not to withdraw from Hebron.

"Now that we all know the Palestinian police are murderers, whoever decides to let these police enter Hebron will be an accomplice to murder and that includes people who are pressuring the government to compromise -- the Israeli left and the U.S. administration," Arnon told Reuters.

Palestinian-ruled cities are not under curfew but travel between them is virtually impossible because of an Israeli blockade. Israel has ringed them with tanks to quell violence if the Washington summit collapses.
Samir Huleileh, Assistant Undersecretary for Trade in the Palestinian Authority, said the Palestinian economy was losing $10 million a day because of the siege.
PLO officials in touch with the Palestinian delegation in Washington were pessimistic.
"So far, so bad," said Arafat aide Marwan Kanafani, attending a sombre session of the Palestinian Legislative Council in Ramallah, scene of some of the fiercest battles.
"We will not hesitate to announce the failure of the summit if there is no practical progress in content," Palestinian minister Hanan Ashrawi said.
